## Ordinal logit as a set of parallel binary regressions

- The assumption of equal slopes in the ordinal model is interchangeably called:
  - Proportional odds assumption
  - Parallel regression assumption
- Suppose *y* has 4 outcomes (e.g. SD, D, A, SA)
- Create 4 - 1 = 3 binary variables

  B~1~=1 if *y* ≤ 1, else 0

  B~2~=1 if *y* ≤ 2, else 0

  B~3~=1 if *y* ≤ 3, else 0

- Fit three binary logits where both intercepts (α) and coefficients (β) can vary across each model:

$$\begin{aligned} \Pr(B_{1}) &= \Pr(y \leq 1) = F(\alpha_{1} + \beta_{1,1}x_{1} + \beta_{2,1}x_{2}) \\ \Pr(B_{2}) &= \Pr(y \leq 2) = F(\alpha_{2} + \beta_{1,2}x_{1} + \beta_{2,2}x_{2}) \\ \Pr(B_{3}) &= \Pr(y \leq 3) = F(\alpha_{3} + \beta_{1,3}x_{1} + \beta_{2,3}x_{2}) \end{aligned}$$

- Ordinal logit simultaneously fits the equations:

$$\begin{aligned} \Pr(y \leq 1) &= F(\alpha_{1} + \beta_{1}x_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{2}) \\ \Pr(y \leq 2) &= F(\alpha_{2} + \beta_{1}x_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{2}) \\ \Pr(y \leq 3) &= F(\alpha_{3} + \beta_{1}x_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{2}) \end{aligned}$$

  - The β's are constrained to be **identical** in all equations
  - The intercepts (α) vary by cumulative outcome (these are the estimates of the thresholds $\tau$)

### Ordinality assumption revisited

- To begin this section, I emphasized the ordinality assumption is about **the relationship between the IVs and the DVs**---it is an assumption about the model, not just about the DV
- Even when your DV is clearly an inherently ordinal DV (e.g., educational degree attainment)---this does not mean your **model** will meet the ordinality assumption
- Consider the graph above: this plots the cumulative probabilities across the range of a continuous IV
  - Some IVs may produce ordinal relationships with the DV
  - Some IVs may not
- Thus, **a DV itself can never satisfy the ordinality assumption** of the model
  - E.g., A DV may pass the assumption in one model or sample, but not an alternative with different IVs, or in a different sample

### Formal tests of parallel regressions

- The **Brant test** determines if the coefficients from individual binary logits equal those from the ordinal logit model where they are all constrained to be equal
  - In Stata, **spost13** command **brant** will calculate this for you; both for each individual IV and an overall test for the model; in R, package [**brant**](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/brant/versions/0.3-0/topics/brant)
- Tests often reject the parallel regression assumption
  - In my experience, they are very sensitive to even minor deviations from perfectly parallel regressions
- If rejected, verify the consequences of the assumption by comparing predictions from the ordinal model with a model that does not impose the parallel regression assumption (e.g., multinomial logit)
  - I would not publish results from ordinal logit when tests indicate a violation of the parallel regression assumption **unless** I can provide explicit evidence it does not bias conclusions

```{.r .cell-code}
gss <- read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_gss.dta")

# Religious attendee = attends about once a month or more
gss <- gss |>
  mutate(religous = case_when(attend <= 3 ~ 0, attend >= 4 ~ 1)) |>
  filter(year >= 1986)

# Keep model variables; drop any missing data
gss <- gss[c("pillok", "year1972", "religous", "college", "age", "woman", "race3", "faminc")]
gss <- gss[complete.cases(gss), ]

# Ordinal DV as a factor with short labels; binary/nominal variables as factors
gss <- gss |>
  mutate(pillok = factor(pillok, levels = 1:4,
      labels = c("StrAgree", "Agree", "Disagree", "StrDisag")),
    religous = factor(religous, labels = c("Not Religious", "Religious")),
    across(c(college, woman, race3), as_factor),
    year1972 = as.numeric(year1972)) |>
  droplevels()

opmod <- polr(pillok ~ year1972 + age + woman + religous + college + race3 + faminc,
  data = gss, Hess = TRUE)

# Test the parallel regression assumption
```

## Comparing ordinal and nominal predictions

- Before blindly accepting or rejecting the ordinal logit model based on a test of parallel regressions, you should also examine whether predictions from the ordinal model differ importantly from those in a model that **does not impose ordinality**

#### Effects of assuming wrong level of measurement

| **Model choice** (assumed level of DV for analysis) | **True level of DV:** Nominal | Ordinal | Continuous\* |
|:------|:------:|:------:|:------:|
| Nominal | **Ideal** | *Inefficient* | *Inefficient* |
| Ordinal | ***Biased*** | **Ideal** | *Inefficient* |
| Continuous | ***Biased*** | ***Biased*** | **Ideal** |

\*I am not distinguishing between interval and ratio variables here

- If outcome is ordinal and model is nominal, it is inefficient, but a safe choice
  - If outcome is nominal but model is ordinal, you will have **biased estimates**
- Here I compare ordinal logit to multinomial logit
  - You could also compare predictions to those from the generalized ordered logit model (see [Section 5.6](5-6-generalized-ordered-logit.qmd))

## Testing predictions and effects across models

- The comparisons of the ordinal and nominal model in this section are informal
  - I.e., I did not conduct any significance tests as to whether the predictions and/or MEs were different across the two models
- [Mize, Doan, and Long (2019)](/research/mize_doan_long_2019_SM.qmd) develop a method that can be used to test for differences across the ordinal and multinomial logit models (see example 6.5 in the article)
  - In Stata, the [**mecompare**](/software/mecompare/examples/model-types.qmd) command automates these tests
  - In R, use [**suest**](/software/suest_r/articles/model-types.qmd) to combine the two model's estimates, and [**avg_comparisons**](https://marginaleffects.com/man/r/comparisons.html) to calculate the MEs to compare

### Omnibus tests of difference

- Similar to the variable-specific Brant test, we can obtain a single omnibus test of whether the two models' marginal effects differ or not
  - This obviates the multiple hypothesis testing issue
  - To do so, test if all of the differences are simultaneously equal to zero with **metest** (**\#**s refer to the ME \# column of **mecompare**)
    - To specify an integer, not a ME, use a **\#** (so **#0** = zero)
